sec.title: Background and Objectives
sec.p: Asciminib is indicated for the treatment of adult patients with newly diagnosed or previously treated Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic phase (Ph+ CML-CP) at a total daily dose of 80 mg, as well as adult patients with Ph+ CML with the T315I mutation at 200 mg twice daily. In patients with the T315I mutation, responses have been observed at doses of ≥150 mg twice daily and dose reduction to 160 mg twice daily is permitted for management of adverse reactions. The objective of this study was to assess the effect of strong CYP3A4 induction, through phenytoin, on the pharmacokinetics (PK) of single dose asciminib 200 mg. Coproporphyrin-1 (CP-1) was also measured to evaluate the effect of asciminib 200 mg on organic anion transporting polypeptide 1B (OATP1B).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This Phase 1 open-label fixed-sequence study evaluated the PK of a single oral dose of asciminib in healthy participants when administered alone and in combination with phenytoin. A single dose of 200 mg asciminib was administered on Day 1, followed by the administration of phenytoin 100 mg three times daily from Day 6 to Day 23, taken 8 h apart to ensure full induction. On Day 20, the morning doses of phenytoin and asciminib were co-administered. Serial blood samples were collected for the assessment of asciminib PK and CP-1 plasma concentrations.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: All 15 participants who enrolled were male and 14 received study treatment per protocol. Following co-administration with phenytoin, asciminib-adjusted geometric mean maximum plasma concentration (Cmax), area under the curve to the last plasma concentration (AUClast) and AUC to infinity (AUC0-inf) were reduced by 22%, 34%, and 34%, with test/reference ratios of 0.780 (90% CI: 0.718–0.847), 0.662 (90% CI: 0.624–0.703), and 0.664 (90% CI: 0.626–0.705), respectively. A single oral dose of asciminib 200 mg did not have a relevant effect on CP-1 plasma exposure.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: These data support that, considering its large therapeutic window, asciminib 200 mg twice daily can be used without any dose adjustment when co-administered with a strong CYP3A4 inducer drug. Furthermore, asciminib is not an OATP1B inhibitor up to this dose.

tr.td: Asciminib is approved in some countries for adult patients with Philadelphia chromosome–positive chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic phase with the T315I mutation at 200 mg twice daily.

This study assessed the effect of strong CYP3A4 induction, through phenytoin, on the pharmacokinetics of single-dose asciminib 200 mg and found that asciminib Cmax, AUClast and AUC0-inf were reduced by 22%, 34%, and 34%, respectively, when given with phenytoin.

This reduction is not considered clinically relevant given the large therapeutic window of asciminib; asciminib 200 mg twice daily can therefore be used without any dose adjustment when co-administered with a strong CYP3A4 inducer drug.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm primarily characterized by the presence of the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome, which leads to the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene, resulting in a constitutively active BCR::ABL1 tyrosine kinase [1, 2]. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) targeting BCR::ABL1 have transformed the CML therapeutic landscape and are currently the treatment of choice for patients with CML [2, 3]. Despite the success of TKIs, clinical resistance through acquisition of mutations in the BCR::ABL1 kinase domain remains a concern. The gatekeeper T315I mutation, reported in 2–20% of patients treated with frontline imatinib and approximately 5% of patients treated with frontline second-generation TKIs [4, 5], confers resistance to most ATP-competitive TKIs and is associated with an unfavorable prognosis [6]. Asciminib is the first BCR::ABL1 inhibitor that specifically targets the ABL myristoyl pocket [7]. The allosteric inhibition of ABL1 means that asciminib can maintain activity against forms of BCR::ABL1 carrying resistance mutations, including the T315I mutation, in the ATP-binding site [8]. In Europe and the USA, asciminib is approved for adult patients with Ph+ CML in chronic phase (CP) [9, 10] and in some countries, including the USA, asciminib is also approved for the treatment of adult patients with Ph+ CML-CP with the T315I mutation [10].

Asciminib does not inhibit the T315I mutation with the same potency as the wild type BCR::ABL1 variant [7, 11]. The proliferation of Luc-Ba/F3 cells engineered to express BCR::ABL1 wildtype was inhibited by asciminib with a mean half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) value of 0.61 nM, compared with 7.64 nM for BCR::ABL1T315I [7]. Although a total daily dose of 80 mg is recommended for patients without the T315I mutation, a higher dose of 200 mg twice daily (bid) is required in patients with the T315I mutation to exert sufficient BCR::ABL1 inhibition [7].

Based on in vitro and clinical human absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion data, asciminib is primarily metabolized through CYP3A4-mediated oxidation (36.0%) and UGT2B7- and UGT2B17-mediated glucuronidation (13.3% and 7.8%, respectively) and biliary secretion via breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) contributes about 31.1% to total systemic clearance [11]. The CYP3A4 inducers are therefore expected to affect the pharmacokinetics (PK) of asciminib and a previous Phase 1 drug-drug interaction (DDI) study was conducted to assess the effect of the CYP3A4 inducer rifampicin on the PK of a single 40-mg oral dose of asciminib in healthy participants. Asciminib exposure (as area under the curve [AUC]) was decreased by ~13–15% with concomitant administration of rifampicin, but this decrease was not considered clinically meaningful considering the large therapeutic window of asciminib [12]. As the approved dose for patients with Ph+ CML-CP with the T315I mutation is five times higher than for patients without the mutation (200 mg bid vs total daily dose of 80 mg) [10], this Phase 1, open-label, DDI study assessed the effect of strong CYP3A4 induction, through phenytoin, on the PK of a single oral dose of asciminib 200 mg in healthy participants. Phenytoin is recognized as a strong inducer of CYP3A4 and serves as an alternative index inducer to rifampicin [13, 14].

In vitro data have suggested that asciminib can inhibit OATP1B transporters [11]. In a clinical DDI study, plasma concentrations of coproporphyrin-1 (CP-1), an endogenous substrate of organic anion transporting polypeptide 1B (OATP1B), were not affected by asciminib 80 mg once daily [15]. An additional objective of the present study was to measure the effect of single-dose asciminib 200 mg on CP-1.

sec.title: Study Design and Treatment Administration
sec.p:
This was a Phase 1, open-label, fixed-sequence, DDI study consisting of a screening period, two treatment periods, and a safety follow-up period of 30 days after the last dose of asciminib (Fig. 1).Fig. 1
Study design. 1EoS defined as the date of the last scheduled procedure. 2A post-study safety contact (e.g., follow-up telephone call or email) occurred approximately 30 days after the last administration of study treatment. EoS end of study, PK pharmacokinetics, tid three times daily

During treatment period 1 (Days 1–5), participants received a single dose of asciminib 200 mg on Day 1 after an overnight fast (for at least 10 h). Participants continued to fast for an additional 4 h post-dose. A 5-day washout period was scheduled between the first dose of asciminib and the first dose of phenytoin. During treatment period 2 (Days 6–24), participants received phenytoin 100 mg three times daily (tid) from Days 6–23, administered approximately 8 h apart (±1 h). On Day 20, the morning dose of phenytoin and asciminib was co-administered under fasted conditions (10 h before dosing), and participants continued to fast for an additional 4 h post-dose (as done on Day 1). The absorption of asciminib is affected by food and therefore needs to be taken in the fasted state at all doses [9, 10]. The phenytoin dosing preceded asciminib dosing by 14 days and continued for 3 days after asciminib dosing to ensure continued maximal CYP3A4 induction through the majority of the asciminib systemic exposure time course.

Participants were confined during the in-clinic study treatment period for up to 25 days and 24 nights. Asciminib and phenytoin were taken orally with approximately 240 mL of water. Additional water was permitted ad lib, except for 1 h before and until 1 h after asciminib administration on Days 1 and 20. No medication other than the study treatment was allowed from the date the participants signed the informed consent until completion of the end-of-study evaluations, except for protocol-allowed concomitant medication and/or any medication that could be required to treat adverse events (AEs).

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Eligible participants were healthy male or female (non-childbearing potential) adults (aged 18–55 years) in good health as determined by no clinically significant findings from medical history, physical examination, vital signs, and laboratory data, and no significant findings from electrocardiogram (ECG) data or electrolytes in blood or urine, including findings not considered clinically significant. Other inclusion criteria were body mass index (BMI) ranging from 18.5 to 29.9 kg/m2, body temperature of 36.0 to 37.5 °C, systolic blood pressure of 100 to 140 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure of 70 to 90 mmHg, and pulse rate ranging from 60 to 90 bpm.

Key exclusion criteria were a history of any clinically significant medical conditions, treatment with investigational drugs within 30 days or longer if required by local regulation (or five half-lives, whichever is longer) before study dosing and contraindications, hypersensitivity, or any previous adverse reactions to the compound, compound class, or excipients of asciminib or phenytoin or other hydantoins (including ethotoin, mephenytoin, and fosphenytoin).

sec.title: Objectives and Endpoints
sec.p: The primary objective of the study was to evaluate the effect of phenytoin as a strong inducer of CYP3A4 on the PK of asciminib following a single oral dose of 200 mg in healthy participants. Primary endpoints were maximum (peak) observed plasma drug concentration following dose administration (Cmax), area under the curve (AUC) from time zero to the last measurable plasma concentration sampling time (AUClast), and AUC from zero to infinity (AUCinf) of asciminib when administered with phenytoin versus asciminib alone. Secondary plasma PK parameters included time to maximum observed plasma drug concentration (Tmax), apparent terminal elimination half-life (T1/2), AUC from time zero to time t (AUC0-t), time that corresponded to the last measurable concentration (Tlast), total apparent body clearance (CL/F), and apparent volume of distribution during the terminal phase (Vz/F) for asciminib.

Secondary objectives were to assess the safety and tolerability of a single oral dose of asciminib 200 mg given alone or concomitantly with phenytoin in healthy participants and to assess trough concentrations of phenytoin. Secondary endpoints were safety endpoints (including vital signs, physical examinations, ECG findings, safety laboratory parameters, AEs coded using Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 27 (MedDRA) and Common Terminology Criteria for AEs version 5.0), and phenytoin plasma Ctrough levels.

Moreover, the effect of a single oral dose of asciminib 200 mg on CP-1, which is an endogenous OATP1B substrate, was assessed as an exploratory endpoint. Coproporphyrin-1 PK parameters were the plasma pre-dose concentration, Cmax, and AUC from time zero to 24 hours (AUC0-24).

sec.title: PK Sampling and Assessments
sec.p: For the assessment of asciminib plasma concentrations, serial blood samples were collected following asciminib administration on Day 1 (treatment period 1) and Day 20 (treatment period 2): pre-dose (0 h) and at 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 24, 36, 48, 72, and 96 h. Pharmacokinetic samples for phenytoin quantitation were collected from Days 16 to 23 before the morning dose. During treatment period 1, CP-1 PK plasma sampling was performed on Day 1 at pre-dose and at 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 24 h post-dose. Plasma concentrations of asciminib, phenytoin, and CP-1 were determined using validated liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry assays, with the lower limit of quantification values of 1.0, 60.0, and 0.05 ng/mL, respectively. The PK parameters were determined from plasma concentration-time data using noncompartmental methods employing Phoenix WinNonlin software, version 8.3, using the actual sampling times.

sec.title: Sample Size and Statistical Analysis
sec.p: The sample size was chosen based on practical considerations and to obtain a desired precision of the 90% confidence interval (CI) around the estimated geometric mean ratio. A conservative intra-coefficient of variation (CV) of 25% was derived from the maximum intra-subject CV% for AUClast, AUCinf, and Cmax from a previous study of asciminib administered with rifampicin [12]. With a sample size of 12 participants, the precision or half width of the 90% CIs for test-reference comparison on the log scale was calculated to extend 0.181 from the observed difference in means. Considering a potential drop-out rate of 20%, a target of 15 participants was selected.

The safety analysis set, which included all participants who received at least one dose of any study treatment (asciminib or phenytoin), was used for safety evaluations. The PK analysis set (PAS) for asciminib (PAS-asciminib) included all participants who provided an evaluable asciminib PK profile for at least one period. The PAS for phenytoin (PAS-phenytoin) included all participants who provided at least one evaluable phenytoin Ctrough value in treatment period 2.

If a participant did not meet the PAS definition, all scheduled concentrations for that participant as well as corresponding parameters were excluded from analyses. Additionally, if adjusted R2 was <0.75 or the percentage extrapolated AUC was >20%, then λ₋z, T1/2, AUCinf, Vz/F, and CL/F were excluded from analyses. Missing values for any PK parameters or concentrations were not imputed and were treated as missing. Drug concentrations below the lower limit of quantitation (LLOQ) were set to zero by the bio-analyst. Concentrations below LLOQ were treated as missing for the calculation of the geometric means and geometric CV%, and as zero for all other calculations including calculation of PK parameters. Participants with missing PK parameters (e.g., AUCinf, AUClast, Cmax) in one but not both periods were included in the mixed model analysis assuming missing at random.

For asciminib Cmax, AUClast, and AUCinf, a linear mixed-effects model was fitted to the log-transformed PK parameters to estimate the effect of phenytoin at steady-state on the PK of a single-dose of asciminib 200 mg. The model included treatment as a fixed factor and participant as a random factor. For each of the PK parameters, a point estimate and the corresponding two-sided 90% CI for the difference between the means of the test (asciminib 200 mg + phenytoin 100 mg tid) and reference (asciminib 200 mg) treatments were calculated. The means were anti-log transformed to obtain the point estimate and the 90% CI for the geometric mean ratio on the original scale. The linear trapezoidal rule was used for all AUC calculations. For asciminib, regression analysis of the terminal plasma elimination phase for the determination of T1/2 included at least 3 data points after Cmax. All statistical analyses were performed using Statistical Analysis System (SAS), version 9.4.

sec.title: Participant Disposition and Baseline Characteristics
sec.p: Fifteen participants were screened and enrolled in the study. All dosed participants completed the study visits but only 14 were dosed as per the protocol. One participant received treatment as per the protocol until Day 15. On Day 16, the participant received only the morning dose of phenytoin 100 mg. As per the investigator’s decision, the dosing of the study treatment was discontinued due to the treatment-emergent AE of contact dermatitis. Collection of this participant’s Day 16 Ctrough data allowed them to remain in the PAS-phenytoin group. However, discontinuation of the remaining Day 16 to Day 23 phenytoin doses excluded the participant from treatment period 2 PAS-asciminib group. Exclusion from this group also rendered this participant ineligible to receive the planned asciminib dose on Day 20. Nevertheless, all 15 participants who participated in the study were included in the safety analysis set and the PK analysis set for asciminib (PAS-asciminib) and for phenytoin (PAS-phenytoin) as all 15 participants provided an evaluable asciminib/phenytoin profile for at least one period.

The median age at baseline was 33 years (range 22–43 years). All participants were male, and most were White (9; 60%). The median BMI (range) and weight (range) were within the protocol-prespecified inclusion criteria (Table 1). No clinically significant findings were found regarding medical history and concurrent medical conditions. Table 1

sec.title: DDI of Asciminib with Phenytoin
sec.p:

The geometric mean Cmax was 3730 and 2870 ng/mL in the absence and presence of phenytoin, respectively, and occurred at a median Tmax of approximately 2 and 3 hours, respectively. Similarly, the geometric mean AUClast was 38,000 and 24,700 ng*h/mL in the absence and presence of phenytoin, respectively, and the corresponding geometric mean AUCinf was 38,200 and 24,800 ng*h/mL. Tlast was 96 hours, and geometric mean T1/2 was approximately 14 hours for both treatment periods. sec.title: Safety
sec.p:
Overall, eight (53.3%) participants reported at least one AE during the study. Two participants reported contact dermatitis, and other AEs were reported in one participant (6.7%) each (Table 5). In total, 14 AEs were reported, the majority of which were grade 1 (13 AEs reported in eight participants), one was grade 2 (constipation reported by one participant and considered related to both asciminib and phenytoin), and no AEs were grade ≥3. One AE led to study treatment discontinuation; one participant experienced a grade 1 AE of contact dermatitis considered related to phenytoin and both study drugs were withdrawn. The AE resolved, and the patient completed all study visits. No AEs led to study discontinuation. The other case of contact dermatitis was considered not related to asciminib or phenytoin. No serious AEs (SAEs) were reported in the study, and no deaths occurred during the study. Table 5

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study was performed to evaluate the effect of strong CYP3A4 induction through phenytoin on the PK of a single oral dose of asciminib 200 mg in healthy participants. Although this study was open to the enrolment of males and females, all study participants were male. Co-administration of phenytoin decreased asciminib AUCinf and Cmax by 34% and 22%, respectively. This decrease was not considered clinically relevant given the large therapeutic window of asciminib [11]. In a Phase 1 dose-escalation study of asciminib in heavily pretreated patients with CML-CP, asciminib was administered once or twice daily at doses of 10 to 200 mg without reaching a maximum tolerated dose [16]. Responses were observed in patients with the T315I mutation at doses of ≥150 mg twice daily [16, 17] suggesting that the decrease in asciminib exposure with a strong CYP3A4 inducer would not be clinically relevant.

A previous investigation into the PK of co-administration of single-dose asciminib 40 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inducer selected rifampicin (or rifampin) as the perpetrator [12]. Concerns over nitrosamine impurities have since led to a halt in the use of rifampicin in clinical DDI studies [13, 14, 18]. Alternative CYP perpetrators have been explored [13], and phenytoin is listed by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a strong inducer for CYP3A4 [19]. Like rifampicin, phenytoin is a strong CYP3A4 inducer, and the reduction in substrate concentration reported in DDI studies is comparable to that of rifampicin. However, in contrast to rifampicin’s excellent and well-established tolerability profile, phenytoin has the potential for significant toxicity, including serious skin reactions and neurological events [14, 18, 20]. To mitigate these risks, the protocol required participants who experienced known phenytoin AEs or other causally related SAEs to discontinue study treatment.

In another Phase 1 study, for a single oral dose of asciminib 40 mg when co-administered with rifampicin, the observed AUCinf geometric mean ratio was 0.851 (90% CI: 0.80–0.90) [12]. The lower dose of 40 mg limits direct comparability to the present study due to the over-proportional PK of asciminib [11]. However, leveraging these data and PK data from multiple ascending dosing and Phase III studies [16, 21], a nonlinear physiologically based PK (PBPK) model was developed and verified for its ability to predict the PK and DDIs of asciminib. The model assumptions and limitations have been previously reported [22]. The PBPK simulations predicted the AUCinf geometric mean ratio for the interaction of higher asciminib doses with rifampicin and predicted a ratio of 0.492 for single-dose asciminib 200 mg. The established asciminib PBPK model was also prospectively applied for the interaction between phenytoin and asciminib 200 mg and predicted a geometric mean AUC0-inf ratio of 0.624 (90% CI: 0.600–0.649) [22], which is in line with the observed AUC0-inf geometric mean ratio of 0.662 (90% CI: 0.624–0.703) in this study. This suggests that the PBPK-derived simulations predicted the clinical impact of CYP3A induction on asciminib PK well, being within the 10% of the observed values [22]. Further, the effect of phenytoin on a single dose of asciminib 40 and 80 mg was simulated and predicted similar AUC0-inf ratios of 0.676 (90% CI: 0.652–0.700) and 0.649 (90% CI: 0.625–0.675), respectively (Novartis, data on file).

An exploratory objective of this study was to assess the effect of a single oral dose of asciminib 200 mg on CP-1. In vitro data suggest that asciminib may inhibit the transporters OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 [11], and the value of CP-1 as a biomarker of OATP1B activity and OATP1B-mediated DDIs has been previously reported. There was no apparent increase in CP-1 observed over time, which suggests that asciminib at this dose does not inhibit OATP1B1 or OATP1B3. This finding is consistent with a recent study that assessed the effect of asciminib at 80 mg once daily at steady state on the PK parameters of a single dose of atorvastatin. Asciminib 80 mg once daily did not appear to affect the overall (AUC0-24) plasma CP-1 exposure and the CP-1 geometric mean AUC0-24 ratio of atorvastatin plus asciminib versus atorvastatin alone was 1.02 (90% CI: 0.98–1.05) [15].

While interpretation of safety findings from this study is limited by the small sample size and short study duration, overall, single doses of asciminib 200 mg administered with and without phenytoin 100 mg tid were well tolerated. Adverse events related to asciminib were consistent with the known safety profile of asciminib in clinical trials of patients with CML [9, 10, 16, 21], and AEs related to phenytoin were consistent with its safety profile [20]. No grade ≥3 AEs, SAEs, or AEs related to ECG findings or vital signs were reported. One participant experienced a grade 1 AE of contact dermatitis related to phenytoin; therefore, both study drugs were withdrawn, all study visits were completed, and the AE was resolved. No other treatment discontinuations due to AEs were observed.

In conclusion, this study builds on previously reported data and provides important DDI results for the coadministration of asciminib 200 mg with strong CYP3A4 inducers. Dose adjustments are not required for asciminib when co-administered with a strong CYP3A4 inducer drug [10], considering its large therapeutic window. The study also complements other evidence to suggest that asciminib is not an OATP1B inhibitor at all marketed doses.
